title: Nirmala learning
hook: Nirmala scholars wrote commentaries explaining Gurbani

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nirmalas: the pure ones, tracing themselves to students sent to study in Benares. Your line was the scholars. What did you learn, and who did you pass it to? Day one thousand three hundred six.

Two people read the same text message. Sounds good. One hears a happy yes. The other hears a tired, flat, fine, whatever. Same two words, two meanings, and the difference lives in something the words don't show. Old texts can do this too, Gurbani among them. A single word can lean two ways. So, for a long time, people have sat down with the Guru's lines and written out, slowly, what each one means. A scholar's explanation like that has a name. Nirmala scholars wrote them. Today: Nirmala learning.
screen: `SOUNDS GOOD: A YES, OR A SIGH?` → `ONE WORD CAN LEAN TWO WAYS.` → `SO SOMEONE WRITES IT OUT.`

segments.voice: The name is teeka: a commentary that walks through a text line by line. A teeka sets out the Guru's line, then the meaning of its words, then what the line is doing, and sometimes other ways to read it. Nirmala scholars wrote teekas and gave spoken explanations called katha, and students of Gurbani have learned from them. Here's the kind of question they worked on. The Japji's first step opens with a line built on the word soch. In paraphrase: by soch, it cannot be reached, even if one does soch a hundred thousand times. Now, soch can mean thinking. Read that way, the line says you can't think your way to God, however hard you think. But soch can also mean ritual cleansing, the bath and the washing that some held made a person pure. Read that way, the line says outward washing, however often, can't make the mind clean. Some readers hear it one way, some the other, and some hold both at once. Notice the link to yesterday's word: nirmal, without stain. Either reading is about what actually makes a person clear. Two more things a teeka does. It's honest when a word is hard, and a careful one lists the readings instead of hiding the choice. And it never replaces the Guru's line. The line stays on top; the explanation sits underneath, in smaller letters, so to speak. Readers can disagree with a teeka. That's allowed, and it's part of the tradition. The point of explaining is to send the reader back to the line with better ears.
screen: `TEEKA: A LINE-BY-LINE COMMENTARY.` · `SOCH: THINKING, OR WASHING?` · `A CAREFUL TEEKA LISTS THE READINGS.` · `THE LINE STAYS ON TOP.` · then, large: `EXPLAINED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one explanation. For now, settle, and breathe. Hold the Japji's line in mind: by soch, it cannot be reached. On one breath, hear it as thinking: you can't think your way there. On the next, hear it as washing: outward cleaning can't clean the mind. Go back and forth, slowly, a reading for each breath. Don't choose. Let both stand. After the bell, find one written explanation of any line of Gurbani, and read it all the way through. The bell holds the time.
Nirmala learning. Teekas and katha: scholars walking line by line through Gurbani, listing the readings, and keeping the Guru's line on top. Today's word.
Your line: explained. Today, when a message or a sentence could lean two ways, ask what the other person meant before you answer. Day one thousand three hundred six.

howItsDone: Sikhs study Gurbani with teekas, written line-by-line commentaries, and katha, spoken explanation in the gurdwara; Nirmala scholars are among those who wrote and taught them.

what a scholar hears: soch in the Japji, thinking or ritual cleansing; readers divide, and some hold both.

notes: Japji pauri 1, 'sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar', paraphrased; 'a hundred thousand times' renders 'lakh vaar' from the text. The two readings of soch (thinking / ritual purity) are well known in Sikh exegesis; please confirm the description and that 'some hold both at once' is fair.

No named Nirmala commentaries or scholars are given, to avoid unverified dates and attributions (e.g., Pandit Tara Singh Narotam). 'Students of Gurbani have learned from them' is general; please confirm or soften.
The script does not claim which reading of soch the Nirmala commentators preferred; please add if a Keeper wishes.
The link to yesterday's 'nirmal, without stain' is the writer's connection, not a claim about the commentaries.
